ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Over-bridges/under-bridges under construction in Assam 
*441. SHRI DWIJENDRA NATH SHAR MAH: Will the Minister of 
RAILWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of over-bridges/under-bridges under construction in Assam; 
(b) the details of the proposals sent by the Government of Assam for 
construction of over-bridges/under-bridges at railway crossings; and 
(c) the steps taken by Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI R. 
VELU): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) Railway takes up works for Road Over/Under Bridges (ROB/RUB) in lieu 
of existing busy level crossings on cost sharing basis where traffic density is 
more than 1 lakh Train Vehicle Units (TVUs) (TVU-A unit obtained by 
multiplying the number of trains with the number of road vehicles passing over the 
level crossing in 24 hours). These works are considered by Railway based on the 
proposals sponsored by State Govt./local bodies duly fulfilling certain preliminary 
requisites. In case of level crossing where traffic density is less than 1 lakh TVUs 
proposals are considered on deposit basis for which initial cost of construction and 
recurring maintenance charges are borne by sponsoring authority. Railway 
construct the railway portion i.e. bridge proper across the railway tracks and 
approaches are completed by State Govt. 

RAJYA SABHA [23 December, 2005] 
At present, one work of construction of ROB in lieu of level crossing No. SK-49 at km 
143/10-11 near Bongaigaon between Salmara and Chapaguri Road stations is under 
construction on cost sharing basis in State of Assam. In addition to above cost sharing 
work, 5 ROB works are under construction on deposit terms. Out of these in case of four 
works entire cost is being borne by. Border Road Organization and in one case entire cost 
is borne by State Govt/PWD. The list of ROB/RUB works under construction on cost 
sharing and deposit terms in Assam State is enclosed as Statement-I (See below) 
(b) No further firm proposal for construction of ROB/RUB in lieu of level crossings has 
been received by railway from Govt, of Assam for inclusion in ensuing Works 
Programme 2006-07 of Railways. 
(c) Does not arise.

Locomotive manufacturing units 
*442. SHRI TARINI KANTA ROY: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the total number of locomotive manufacturing units and their production capacity; 
(b) whether there are other production units outside the PSU's and if so, the details 
thereof; 
(c) whether his Ministry utilizes the full capacity of the production units; 
 
(d) whether the production in Chittaranjan Locomotive Works has decreased 
during the last five years; and 
(e) if so,the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI R. 
VELU): 
(a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) There are two locomotive manufacturing units. Chittaranjan Locomotive 
Works (CLW), Chittaranjan manufactures Electric locomotives aUd Diesel Locomotive 
Works (DLW), Varanasi manufactures Diesel locomotives. The yearly production 
Capacity of CLW is 150 locomotives and of DLW is 150 locomotives. 
(b) Indian Railway's requirements are being fully met from CLW and DLW in the 
recent past. However M/s Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited and M/s SAN 
Engineering Company, Bangalore have supplied electric and narrow gauge diesel 
locomotives respectively, to Indian Railways in the past. In addition, Golden Rock 
workshop, Southern Railway, Trichy and Parel workshop, Central Railway, Mumbai 
are also manufacturing a very limited number of Narrow gauge locomotives. 
(c) Yes Sir, the production plan for 2005-06 is 128 locomotives at CLW against the 
installed capacity of 150 and 143 locomotives at DLW against the installed capacity of 
150. The production plan more or less matches with the available capacity. 
6 

[23 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) No, Sir. The level of Electric Locomotive production at CLW is showing 
an increasing trend except during the year 2002-03, when production was 
less in comparison to production in 2001-02. The figures are as under:— 
Year Production 
2001-02 82 
2002-03 69 
2003-04 86 
2004-05 90 
2005-06 128 (Target) 
(e) Does nor arise. 
SHRI TARINI KANTA ROY: Sir, I thank the Railway Minister for giving 
this reply. Part (c) of the question is whether his Ministry utilises the full 
capacity of the production units and the answer is 'Yes'. But my point is that the 
full capacity of the Railways is not fully utilised because I have the data with me. 
The Minister has also given the data. I have with me the data of 2000-01 also. The 
production was 120 locomotives. In the year 1998-99, Chittaranjan 
manufacturing unit produced 165 locomotives. Then, in 2000-01, it was 120. 
Now, it has decreased. It has the capacity of producing 150 a year, but the Railways 
have ordered only 148 for this year. So, the capacity of production is not fully 
utilised. I don't know what is the cost behind it. Now, he may answer it. 
SHRI R. VELU: Sir, the hon. Member is correct in saying that the capacity 
is 150 units. Our production target this year is 120 units. Why? That is because, 
in the Tenth Plan our whole programme for electrification is of about 1800 KMs. 
The demand for electrical locos has reduced. And, after all, I cannot produce 
more. I am not able to export electrical locos, as I do in the case of diesel locos. 
That is not the priority in the Tenth Plan, with the result, my electrification 
process also is only 27 per cent of my total route kms. in the country. That 
being the case, the demand is less. So, I have to necessarily peg my supply in 
accordance with the demand. So, the point is well-taken. We will definitely 
improve because that has higher priority; because of the diesel prices going up, the 
electrical process will also go up. We will see to it that capacity utilisation is 
improved. 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [23 December, 2005] 
. SHRI TARINI KANTA ROY: My second supplementary is this. As the hon. 
Minister has replied there are two manufacturing units. One is the CLW and 
the other is the DLW. I wish to know whether certain components required by these 
units are obtained through import. If so, what is the total import and what is the 
percentage of that to the total production of these units. 
SHRI R. VELU: Sir, I am not denying the fact that we have been importing 
electrical units. In fact, we imported 30 units. On the diesel side, we imported 
31. But it is only a small number which is why we are importing them. Based on 
that, we are trying to indigenise our own production. In fact, on the electrical 
side, we have made our own electrical motors; 97 per cent are indigenous. 
The result is that as compared to 33 locos that we had been producing on the 
electrical side earlier, today it is only worth 12.5crores, almost one-third, which 
means that the import is meant only for developing our own locos and motors. 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Sir, I cannot understand how the Railway 
Minister can suddenly plan to increase its electrical locomotive production from 
90 to 128 units, because the past record is that they cannot produce that many. 
What steps are they taking to increase this production? Secondly, why is there 
no demand for these either for export or for domestic use? The Railway Ministry 
has completely stopped buying wagons which are used for locomotives. No 
wagon which is good for single-use is being purchased. Wagons only for rake-
loads are being produced. Obviously, the demand has gone down. In the 
process, the villages, the rural areas are suffering because: wagons for single-use 
basis are not available. 
SHRI R. VELU: Sir, it is not factually correct, saying that we cannot 
produce. We had produced 155 wagons in 1996-97, and 165 in 1997-98. Even in 
2002-03, we produced 120. So, the figure of 120 is not an unimaginable 
target. In fact, my capacity is of 150 units. That can be done. 
The other point raised was this. Why are we not exporting and why are we not 
making for the local market? In fact, we have tied up with the ABB of 
Switzerland for electrical motors. We have now got that kind of cooperation. 
Secondly, we are also finding or exploring the market inside the country of non-
rail users. We will also do our best possible to export. I have already mentioned 
that, on the diesel side, we are doing it. For 
8

Malaysia, Tanzania, Sudan, etc. So, we will definitely take that into

SHRI R. VELU: Of course, this is not related to the main question, 
because we are only on the locomotives.  But I will get back to the hon.

through you, I want to mention that this is not at all a high priority. We will

Statement 
The Fifth Central Pay Commission had recommended that study leave should 
be enhanced to three years for all doctors since the duration of the Post-graduate 
(P.G.) courses has been increased to three years. The matter was examined. In view 
of the fact that all Ph.D /P.G. courses are of a maximum period of 36 months 
and combination of leave of other kind due and admissible to an officer in 
continuation of study leave of 24 months is admissible up to a period of 36 months 
and also that the period is considered to be sufficient for such courses, it was 
decided not to increase the period of study leave from the existing two years to 
three years in respect of doctors. 
PROF. P. J. KURIAN; Sir, we want better qualified doctors. Especially in the 
medical field, this is the order of the specialisation. Medical tourism is also on the 
increase. Therefore, the policy of the Government should be to encourage the 
doctors to improve their qualification. But what has the Government done? 
Even while the Fifth Pay Commission had recommended that the three-year 
leave, which is needed for higher education, PG course, should be given to the 
doctors, the Government has given only two-year leave and that too clubbing 
the two years with other eligible links. Instead of encouraging the doctors to 
go for higher education, the Government is giving a disincentive. I would like 
to know while it is the Government's duty to encourage the doctors to improve 
their qualification, what is the rationale and justification for doing this disincentive 
to the doctors. 
DR. ANBUMANI RAMDOSS: Sir, the Health Ministry, in fact, 
recommended to the Department of Personnel and Training (DOPT) to give 
three-year leave for studying the post-graduate course, but then the DOPT had 
their own reservations since there are other Ministries and other Departments, 
they also wanted same procedure done there. So, they had written back stating 
that it is little difficult and already two years had been provided as leave, and 
there was a provision whereby leave could be obtained through other sources, 
like earned leave, for three-year peri od for doing a post-graduate course. 
Meanwhile, we have written to the DOPT again stating that in certain post-
graduate courses, like social and preventive medicine, physiology, bio-
chemistry, M.D. (Psychiatry), etc., where we want a lot more doctors, whether a 
person is a doctor who has already se rved for a three-year period in the 
Government, could be given a

milk products to make them safe in domestic market as well as more

ernment of India to study the improvements required in the existing crop

Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance for 'in principle' approval. The 
Planning Commission and the Ministry of Finance have given some suggestions

3387. SHRI VIJAYARAGHAVAN: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Supreme Court has direct ed after the year 2002 to ensure 
availability and affordability of essential drugs; 
(b) if so, the details of steps taken for the above;

control list of medicine;

THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM VILAS 
PASWAN) (a) to (g) The Government announced the 'Pharmaceutical Policy 2002' in 
February 2002. However, a public interest litigation filed in the High Court of 
Karnataka at Bangalore resulted in an Order dated 12-11-02, which stopped the 
Government from implementing the price control regime of the Pharmaceutical 
Policy 2002. This Department filed a Special Leave Petition (SLP) before the 
Supreme Court of India against the Order of the Karnataka High Court, which 
has been admitted as SLP (C) No. 3668/ 2003. The Supreme Court vide its 
order dated 10.3.2003 directed the Government, inter-alia, that, "we suspend the 
operation of the order to the extent it directs that the Policy dated 15.2.2002 shall 
not be implemented. However we direct that the petitioner shall consider and 
formulate appropriate criteria for ensuring essential and life saving drugs not to 
fall 
94 

[23 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
out of the price control and further directed to review drugs, which are 
essential and life saving in nature till 2nd May, 2003". Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare has brought out the National List of Essential Medicines, 
2003 after the review of the National Essential Drugs List, 1996. The matter 
is sub-judice before the Supreme Court. 
The National Common Minimum Programme as adopted by the 
Government aims, inter-alia, to ensure availability of life saving drugs at 
reasonable prices. In the light of National common Minimum Programme and 
the observations of the Supreme Court in SLP (C) No. 3668/2003, the 
Government constituted a Committee under the Chairmanship of Joint 
Secretary (PI) to suggest measures fo r fulfilling the objectives of National 
Common Minimum Programme to ensure the availability of life saving drugs at 
reasonable prices. This Committee has submitted its interim report to the 
Government. 
Subsequently, a Task Force under the Chairmanship of Dr. Pronab Sen, Principal 
Adviser, Planning Commission was constituted to explore options other than price 
control to make available life saving drugs at reasonable prices. The Task Force 
has submitted its report to the Government on the 20th September, 2005. 
However, the Government in consultation with various stakeholders is 
examining the recommendations of the Task Force. Based on that a new 
Pharmaceutical Policy is likely to be announced shortly.

constitute Vigilance Committee at the State, District, Block and

†3398. SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: 
SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJITHA: 
Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that administrative expenditure is more under the 
targeted Public Distribution System; 
(b) if so, whether it is also a fact that to provide benefit of Re. 1 to needy poor 
person, Rs. 3.65 are spent; 
(c) if so, the facts in this regard; and 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
108 

[23 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) whether there exists a need to re duce the said expenditure and if so, 
Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (DR. AKHILESH PRASAD 
SINGH): 
(a) The Programme Evaluation Organisation (PEO) of the Planning 
Commission has conducted the performance Evaluation on targeted Public 
Distribution System (TPDS). In the Study report, the administrative expenditure 
for TPDS was not separately estimated. However, the said Report shows that the 
actual income gain to a BPL household purchasing food grains from PDS was 
only 65% of the budgetary income transfer made to him. This was an 
indication of the high cost of administration of PDS. 
(b) The estimates drawn by PEO was based on a sample survey of 18 States in 
the country, show that only 42.17% of the subsidized food grains meant for the 
population below poverty li ne (BPL) reached them. While this figure is 
combined with the figure on relative efficiency of PDS given in (a) above, it turns 
out that for a budgetary income transfer of Re.1/- to the poor, the Government 
spent Rs. 3.65/- [i.e. Re. 1/ (0.4217x0.65)]. 
(c) The gap reported above was primarily due to , (i) the high cost of 
handling food grains incurred by the agencies involved therein (reflected in the 
trade-of between budgeted income transfer and actual income gain to a poor PDS 
consumer) are (ii) the leakages/diversion of BPL grains from the distribution 
chain. The aforesaid leakages include: 
 
* The diversion of good grains meant for the poor to the non-poor on 
account of the overestimation of the number of poor households 
(estimated to be 21.45% of the total subsidized grains). 
* Leakage through deliberately created ghost ration cards, i.e. Cards not with 
their actual owners and excess cards within the system (estimated to be 
16.67%) and Leakage of BPL food grains at the FPS level (Estimated to 
be 19.71%) It was further noted that ; (i) the FPS level profits were 
extremely low in general on account of low margins allowed to them 
and low volume of transactions and (ii) the mechanism put in place for 
monitoring distribution of PDS grains was weak across states. 
109 

RAJYA SABHA [23 December, 2005] 
(d) Due to all the above, there existed the need for reducing the admin-istrative 
expenditure of public agencies involved in grain handling and for plugging the leakages of 
BPL good grains from their supply chain.

3408. SHRI S.M. LALJAN BASHA: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT

reaches of rivers;

negatively affected by such un-planned construction; 
(e) whether any inspection has been done till date; and 
(f) if so, the details in this matter? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) to (0 A representation 
from Chairman, Forum on Special and Human Rights is reported to have been 
received in the Union Ministry of Power raising certain points relating to the 
construction of transmission towers across rivers by Power Grid Corporation 
of India Ltd. (PGCIL) in general and across Godavari river in particular. This 
representation was sent by the Ministry of Power to PGCIL.The PGCIL after 
examining the matter is reported to have informed that rivers enroute the 
transmission lines are normally crossed by placing towers on the banks of the river 
and in case where the width of the river is large, mid-stream towers are provided 
on pile or well foundations. As the 
117 

RAJYA SABHA [23 December, 2005] 
size of the structure is small, they do not alter the river currents/free flow of 
water in a river and as such pose no environmental concerns. These foundations 
are generally constructed away from perennial river streams to avoid obstruction 
to navigation and danger to boats and steamers.

struction of transmission line is taken up as per the programme of planned 
development in the transmission syst em. Where it is necessary to have 
transmission line across rivers, very high towers of special designs are used for 
river crossing so as to avoid towers in lower reaches of rivers. The towers in the 
lower reaches of rivers require pile foundtion involving extra expenditure and 
therefore, such towers are minimized to the extent possible and as such there is 
no unplanned construction of power transmission towers in the lower reaches of 
the rivers. By adopting high towers of special designs, long span across the river 
is achieved, so that the safety of the towers as well as the flow of the river is not 
affected.

Change of climates 
†3421. DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: 
SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the climate of the country is changing now a days; 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that due to this change of climate, forests and 
lives of people and animals living in the forests are likely to be affected; and 
(d) if so, the facts of the matter and the steps being taken by Government? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) As per information made 
available by the Indian Meteorol ogical Department, the surface air 
temperature over the Indian subcontinent show a slightly warming trend by 
about 0.4 C during the past 100 years. This warming trend is however 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
131 

RAJYASABHA [23 December, 2005] 
not uniform either in time or space. Some seasons do not exhibit as much warming 
trend as the others, and some regions of the country show lesser warming trend. 
However, Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) in its Third Assessment 
Report in 2001 has projected that globally averaged surface temperature would rise 
by 1.4 C to 5.8 C during 1990—2100 in the most tropical and subtropical 
regions. 
(b) The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change 
(UNFCCC) and the Kyoto Protocol address the issues related to climate change. 
India is a Party to both these agreements and is actively participating in Climate 
Change discussions. India has taken meas ures to mitigate climate chage by 
encouraging renewable sources of energy, energy efficiency, afforestation 
programmes and promoting projects under the Clean Development Mechanism 
(CDM) of the Kyoto Protocol, which reduce net emissions of greenhouse gases. 
(c) and (d) The project climate change will affect various ecosystems 
including forests and lives of people and animals living in the forests only on a 
long term basis. In the short term, the effect of global climate change on forests, 
wildlife and people living close to forests is likely to be insignificant.

[23 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAM-
ILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) As per Iodine De-
ficiency Disorders (IDD) surveys conducted by Directorate General of Health 
Services, State Health Directorates, Indian Council of Medical Research and 
other health institutions, no state in the country is free from the problem of 
iodine deficiency disorders. It is estimated that about 7.1 crore people are

disease, alzheimer's disease, retinal degeneration and muscular dystrophy etc. 
(b) Yes, Sir. Various countries including US, UK, Korea, China and Singapore 
have shown interest is having collaborative activities in the area of stem cell research. 
(c) The Government has taken action for the promotion of research in the field of 
stem cell research and India has emerged as one of the major countries involved in Stem 
Cell Research. According to the Indian Council of Medical Research around 15 institutions 
and three premier health centres in the country are involved in stem cell research and 
related activities. Some of these are: 
 
• The Institute of Immunohaematology, Mumbai under the Indian Council of 
Medical Research (ICMR) undertaking peripheral blood stem   cell   therapy   
in   aplastic   anaemia   patients; 
• The All India Institute of Medical Science, New Delhi involved in clinical 
studies on stem cell therapies particularly in cardiovascular disease; 
• The L.V. Prasad Eye Institute, Hyderabad successful in

RAJYA SABHA [23 December, 2005] 
transplanting a stem cell derived cornea to a patient who had lost his 
cornea; 
• The National Brain Research Centre, Gurgaon involved extensively on 
neural stem cell useful in several congenital and acquired disorder, 
including Parkinson's disease; 
• The National Centre for Cell Sciences, Pune has been working on 
developing a repository of cell cultures and cell lines, cryo-
preservation technology for bone marrow and development of skin for 
burns and vitiligo patients.

(d) and (e) Draft guidelines on regulatory aspects of stem cell research was 
prepared by the Indian Council of Medical Research in 2002 and put on the

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (f) The Candian 
Government has recently imposed a ban on the 10 Indian Ayurvedic and Unani 
medicinal products on the ground that they contain high levels of metals such 
as lead, mercury and/or arsenic. No su ch ban has been imposed by U.K. and 
European Union on Indian Ayurvedic Medicines. Indian Ayurvedic products 
have always been sold as food supplements in the EU market. The recent Directive 
2004/24/EC which has caused some concern is in fact only an amendment to the

products for human use to harmonise and put on fast track the registration of

medicines has been taken up with the European Union.

from January 1, 2006 providing for mandatory testing for heavy metals for 
Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani medicines which are to be exported. Orders have 
also been issued to all State Licensing Authorities to ensure that all Ayurveda, 
Siddha, Unani drug manufacturing units become Good Manufacturing Practices 
compliant and that they should display on the container of a medicine or a leaflet 
inside the container the names and quantities of all ingredients used in the

3448. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the recent press reports that AIDS 
epidemic infections in India in 2004 was just 28000 as against 6 lakhs in the

176

(b) if so, whether this huge reduction is attributable to multi-faceted 
measures adopted in creating in awareness in public or whether there are other 
reasons therefor; and 
(c) what was the projection of such cases in 2004 and how many such cases 
have come to light in the first three months of 2005? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The 
year-wise estimated number of infections for the year 2002, 2003, and 2004 
are as follows:  
Year Estimated number of 
 infections 
2002 45.80 lakh 
2003 51.06 lakh 
2004 51.34 lakh 
However, it may be mentioned that in India, HIV Sentinel Surveillance (HSS) 
was initiated in 1998 with the objective of monitoring the growth of the infection 
among high-risk group and extent of spread to the general population. 
Accordingly a few sentinel sites we re established in places where HIV 
infections were found prevalent. In the absence of any other reliable data, HSS 
data was utilized to estimate the probable number of infections in the country 
based on certain assumptions. These assumptions were based on the available 
literature and experience of eminent epidemiologists and biostatisticians of 
national and international repute and the experts from WHO and UNAIDS. 
The HSS has been expanded to get more representative data and the 
assumptions used for estimation have been validated based on available 
epidemiological data, viz., community based national survey to estimate the 
prevalence of STD in India, and validation of assumptions using HSS data. 
Thus the year-wise figures are no t comparable. The data from HSS 
indicate that there is a mixed response of the epidemic in the country. While 
HIV prevalence is increased in some sub-groups, it has shown early signs of 
sero-stability in States like Tamil Nadu indicating that there is no upsurge of 
HIV epidemic in the country. 
177 

RAJYA SABHA [23 December, 2005] 
(c) National AIDS Contro l Organization conducts annual HIV sentinel 
surveillance (HSS) every year. The estimate based on 2004 HSS was 5.134 
million infections in the country. As per the info rmation received from State

WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANA3AKA LAKS HMI): (a) to (c) A statement

Health is primarily a State subject and provision of medical relief for 
various diseases through primary and community health centres is looked after by 
the State Governments. Communicable diseases are linked to maintenance of 
environmental hygiene, sanitation, consumption of safe and good drinking 
water. The preventive measures taken by local health authorities include provision 
of safe drinking water, improvement of personal and community hygiene, safe 
disposal of human excreta, undertaking appropriate health education, 
surveillance and monitoring, distribution of chlorine tablets and ORS packets 
etc. 
The Government of India supplem ents the efforts of the State 
Governments/Union Territories through various National Health Programmes. 
Funds are also provided under the Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme, 
Accelerated Urban Water Supply Prog ramme, Total Sanitation Campaign,

Stem cell research 
3450. SHRI AVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the discussions with policy-makers and science-administrators 
in Singapore and South Korea on the prospects for collaboration in the area of 
stem cell research were held at the ministerial level, recently; 
(b) if so, the details of issues discussed in the meeting; 
(c) the outcome thereof; 
(d) whether India had set objective to emerge as a global hub for stem ceil 
research; 
(e) if so, the details thereof; 
(f) whether Government have initiated the process of mutual recognition 
of doctors, nurses and dentists under the recently signed India-Singapore 
Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement; and 
(g) if so, the complete details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (c) A delegation led 
by Hon'ble Minister of Health and Family Welfare recently visited Korea and 
Singapore. The delegation met the Korean Minister of Health and discussed 
future areas of collaboration, including stem cell research, between India and 
Korea. Letters of intent have also been received from Histo Stem Inc., Korea and 
Histo Stem Inc., Delaware, USA wherein it is proposed to set up Cord Blood 
Stem Cell Banking network in India to store stem cells as well as to coordinate 
research for the development of Stem Cell therapies to treat various 
malignancies and diseases. 
(d) and (e) India has emerged as one of the major countries involved in Stem. 
Cell Research. Indian Council of  Medical Research (ICMR) and 
Department of Bio-Technology are promoting stem cell research. Around 15 
institutes and 3 premier health centres in the country are involved in stem cell 
research and related activities funded by different funding agencies

like Department of Science and Technology, Department of Bio-Technology and 
ICMR. Some of these institutes are: 
• The Institute of Immunohaematology, Mumbai under the Indian 
Council of Medical Research (ICMR) undertaking peripheral blood stem 
cell therapy in aplastic anaemia patients; 
• The All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi involved in 
clinical studies on stem cell therap ies particularly in cardiovascular 
diseases; 
• The L.V. Prasad Eye Institute, Hyderabad successful in transplanting 
a stem cell derived cornea to a patient who had lost his cornea; 
• the National Brain Research Centre, Gurgaon involved extensively on 
neural stem cell useful in severa l congenital and acquired disorder, 
including Parkinson's disease;

developing a repository of cell cultures and cell lines, cryo-
preservation technology for bone marrow and development of skin for 
burns and vitiligo patients.

umbilical cord blood stem cell, they are also setting up various blood stem cell

Blood Repository in June, 2000. Recen tly Asia Cryo-cell in collaboration 
with Florida based Cryo-cell International has set up India's first Umbilical Cord 
Blood Stem Bank with 24 collection centres across the country near Chennai. 
The ICMR has also proposed to establish Cord Blood Stem Cell Banks in seven 
regional centres with coordinating unit at ICMR's Institute of 
Immunohaematology (IIH), Mumbai.

Cardiovascular diseases among urban population in Delhi 
3451. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a study by the Indian Council of Medical Research in 
collaboration with the Cardiology Department of All India Institute of Medical 
Sciences revealed that the urban population in Delhi is more prone to cardio 
vascular diseases than its rural counterparts as the former is more prone to the 
risk factors in comparison to the latter; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether it is a fact that the chan ging lifestyle and habits are the 
contributory factors to this growing menace among the urban populace; and 
(d) if so, the steps being taken by Government to improve the situation among 
the urban population by introducing novel methods? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKS HMI): (a) Indian Council of 
Medical Research in collaboration with the Cardiology Department of All India 
Institute of Medical Sciences had carried out a cross-sectional study titled "ICMR 
Task force Project on collaborative study of coronary heart diseases" in 
individuals aged 35-64 years from 1991-1994. The department of Cardiology 
(AIIMS) and CMC (Vellore) were the participating centres in the study. From the 
data it has been observed that the pr evalence of coronary heart disease, 
hypertension and distribution of associated factors (such as smoking, physical 
activity, cholesterol, triglycerides etc.) related to coronary heart disease were 
higher in urban population compared to rural population at Delhi and Vellore. 
(b) to (d) The reasons attributed for hi gher cardiovascular risk factor levels 
in the urban areas are reflective of the marketdly different lifestyles in urban and 
rural India. Rural residents, with marginal infrastructure for transport and other 
lifestyle comforts, necessarily adopt an active life style. This is also associated with 
consumption of locally available food products. On the contrary, urban residents 
are far more likely to have a sedentary lifestyle with adverse nutritional 
practices. 
Government have initiated awareness programme through media and IEC 
activities. Attention has been given on Yoga through AYUSH.

New guidelines for processed food items 
3462. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether his Ministry proposes to make it mandatory for the 
manufacturers of processed food items to mention the details of the ingredients 
on the labels including the fat content and the technique used in its manufacture and 
storage; and 
(b) if so, the details of the new rules and when they are likely to be 
implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The 
Central Committee for Food Standards a statutory committee under the Prevention 
of Food Adulteration (PFA) Act, 1954 recommended the amendment of PFA 
Rules, 1955 to declare the complete nutritional information of the food product on 
its label. The information is recommended to be given on the label shall be in the 
following format:— 
"The complete nutritional information per 100 gm of the product shall be given on 
the label containing the following:— 
(i) Information on energy value should be expressed in kJ and Kcal per 100 
gm or per 100 ml alongwith percentage of nutrient of Recommended 
Dietary Allowance (RDA) of Indi an Council of Medical Research 
(ICMR). 
(ii) Information on the amounts of prot ein, carbohydrate and fat in the food 
should be expressed in gm per 100 gm or per 100 ml alongwith percentage 
RDA of nutrient recommended by ICMR. 
(iii) The amount and/or type of fatty saturated fatty acids, polyunsaturated 
fatty acids and trans fatty acids. 
(iv) Numerical information on vitamins and minerals should be expressed in 
metric units and/or as a percentage of the Nutrient Reference Value of 
ICMR per 100 gm or per 100 ml alongwith percentage of nutrient of 
RDA of ICMR." 
The above proposal has been published in Part II, Section 3, Sub-section (i) of the 
Gazette of India (Extraordinary) vide GSR No. 694 (E) dated 
198 

[23 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
28.11.2005 for inviting objections and suggestions from the public. While 
finalizing the draft rules, the objections and suggestions received on the draft 
rules would be taken into consideration after a period of sixty days from the 
date on which the copies of the Official Gazette in which this notification is 
published are made available to public.

sanctioned strength includes not only the bare requirement for operation but also Rest Givers, 
Leave Reserve and provision for training etc. In the case of category of Drivers, these 
additional provisions are upto 30% which take care of gaps, if any, between occurrence and

Demand for legal framework on pastoral rights in the country 
SHRI E.M. SUDARSANA NATCHIAPPAN (Tamil Nadu): Sir, 
pastoralists are conservers of domestic animal biodiversity and due to their 
traditional life style they contribute to the ecology and economy of our nation. 
Therefore, there is a st rong need to recognise their conservation culture 
practised by them. Pastoralists should not be marginalized or designated as 
destroyers of forests in the name of r egeneration of forests by initiating 
bilateral programmes such as Joint Forest Management or wild life sanctuary. 
Pastoralists should be integrated in holistic, joint co-existence conservation 
approaches by using their knowledge in natural resource management. 
Biological Diversity Act, 2002 stipul ates "conservation, sustainable 
use of biological diversity including in situ conservation of breeds of domestic 
animals under their surrounding natural habitat." 
As a signatory to the United Nations Convention on Biological 
Diversity,   India  has  committed  itself to  respect,   preserve  and  maintain 
320 

[23 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
knowledge, innovations and practices of indigenous and local communities 
embodying traditional lifestyles relevant  for the conservation and sustainable 
use of biological diversity. 
As a matter of the Durban Action Plan (2004), which is the outcome 
of Vth IUCN World Parks Congress (Septe mber 2003), it is a mandate for our 
country "in securing the rights of indigenous people, including mobile 
indigenous people, and local communities in relation to natural resources and 
biodiversity conservation." 
The Draft Scheduled Tribes (Recognition of Forest Rights) Bill, 2005, 
envisages "rights of use or  entitlements such as grazing in forests and 
traditional seasonal resource access of nomadic or pastoralist communities." 
Therefore, Government of India has  to seriously consider, recognise 
and protect the role of pastoralists/her ders conferring the following rights 
which will go a long way towards community conservation of domestic animal 
biodiversity.   Thank you.

SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAI (Chhatti sgarh): Sir, malaria is re-
emerging as the number one killer disease in Chhattisgarh. It has reported the 
third highest malaria cases in the country. But despite being endemic,

Chhattisgarh has a high prevalence of malaria because of highly 
dense forests and vast area of paddy fields, which allow mosquitoes to breed

year. There are 4500 patients in Sarguja and over 3000 patients in Ambikapur.

the last two years alone. But, local people say many deaths go unreported 
because they take place in remote areas.

parasite. And, till a vaccine is developed, precaution is the best cure.

vaccines.

Housa present that today we are sitting in a very unusual and an

be a court of honour, but there is so mething common between a court of law
